n: Chapter 2 begins by reversing the children’s names: call your brothers Ammi (“my people”) and your sisters Ruhamah (“loved”). Some translations place this verse at the end of chapter 1, as the conclusion of its promise.
Now the Lord speaks like a wronged husband in court, urging the children to plead with their mother (Israel) to give up her unfaithfulness. The marriage is broken—but He still wants her back.

f.w: she is not my wife, neither am I her husband
f.g: Language resembling a divorce declaration, though the goal is reconciliation.

n: If she does not change, she will be stripped bare and left like a desert—a picture of the land’s devastation in war and drought.

f.w: set her as in the day that she was born

n: Her children, sharing her unfaithfulness, will share her fate. The people of Israel are both the wife and the children in this extended metaphor.
Israel credited her “lovers”—the Baal gods and foreign allies—for her food, clothing, and oil. Baal was the Canaanite storm god believed to give rain and fertility.

f.g: Baal and other gods (and perhaps foreign alliances) Israel trusted for prosperity.

n: God will block her path with a thorn hedge and wall, so she can’t find her way to her lovers. His “obstacles” are acts of love meant to turn her back.

f.w: I will hedge up thy way with thorns

n: Frustrated in chasing her lovers, she will say, “I’ll go back to my first husband; I was better off then”—like the prodigal son who came to himself.

f.w: I will go and return to my first husband

n: She never realized that it was the Lord who gave her grain, wine, and oil—and the silver and gold she used for Baal worship.

f.w: she did not know that I gave her corn, and wine, and oil

f.g: Used to make idols or offerings for Baal.

n: So God will take back His gifts at harvest time, showing who truly provides.

f.g: At harvest time, when she expects it.

n: He will expose her shame before her lovers, who will be powerless to rescue her.
Her celebrations will cease—festivals, new moons, and Sabbaths—because her worship had become empty and mixed with idolatry.

f.w: her feast days, her new moons, and her sabbaths

n: The vines and fig trees she called payment from her lovers will become wild thickets eaten by animals.
God will punish her for the feast days of the Baals, when she dressed up with jewelry to chase other gods and forgot Him. Forgetting God is the root sin.

f.g: Plural of Baal—the various local Baal gods.

n: Here the chapter turns. Instead of final rejection, God will woo Israel back, lead her into the wilderness as in the Exodus, and speak tenderly to her heart. This is the heart of Hosea’s message: God’s relentless, redeeming love.
The valley of Achor (“trouble”)—where Achan sinned and was punished—will become a door of hope. Israel will respond as she did as a young bride coming out of Egypt.

f.w: as in the days of her youth

n: Israel will call God Ishi (“my husband”) rather than Baali (“my master”)—a relationship of love, not mere ownership, and free from any confusion with Baal.

f.g: Hebrew “my master” or “my Baal”—a word also used for husband, but tainted by idolatry.

n: God will remove the names of the Baals from her lips; they won’t even be remembered.

f.w: I will take away the names of Baalim

n: God will make a covenant of peace with all creation and abolish war. Israel will rest securely—a picture of the Millennium.

f.w: make a covenant for them with the beasts of the field
I will break the bow and the sword

n: “I will betroth you to Me forever.” God offers a brand-new marriage covenant, with gifts of righteousness, justice, steadfast love, and compassion. In ancient times the groom paid a bride-price—here God Himself provides the gifts.

f.w: I will betroth thee unto me for ever

n: He will betroth her in faithfulness, and she will “know the LORD”—an intimate, personal knowledge, the goal of the covenant.
In that day God will answer the heavens, and the heavens will answer the earth—a chain of blessing as rain falls again.
The earth will answer with grain, wine, and oil, and they will answer Jezreel (“God sows”). Everything Israel sought from Baal now comes from God.
God will “sow” Israel in the land, show mercy to Lo-ruhamah, and say to Lo-ammi, “You are My people,” and they will answer, “You are my God.” Every name of judgment is reversed into a name of grace.

f.w: I will say to them which were not my people, Thou art my people
I will sow her unto me in the earth
